title: Logos e-commerce
description: A microservices experiment inspired by the principle of Logos (the rational order of the universe) in Stoic philosophy.
body: A microservices architecture built for absolute resilience. 'Order in chaos.' Driven by Logos (Universal Logic), ensuring every service stands firm, scales independently, and survives the noise of high-traffic commerce.

star.situation: I myself spent a lot of time learning the concept of kubernetes and containers, and even then it was easy to forget, so I created an e-commerce that utilizes containers and kubernetes.
star.task: Design a resource architecture that leverages containers and Kubernetes to create applications that run under desired state.
star.action: Each service is modeled with intent, not ambition. I select the technology stack to fit the problem, not to showcase preference. Excess is a liability; simplicity survives longer. Testing is not an afterthought — unit tests define the boundaries of correctness and guard against quiet regressions.
star.result: The system runs in a controlled, reproducible state, where deployments are predictable and failures are contained rather than disruptive. Services remain observable, testable, and replaceable without affecting the whole. The architecture holds under iteration — not because it is complex, but because it is disciplined. Stability is no longer assumed; it is continuously verified.

technicalFailures.title: Schema Rewrite
technicalFailures.what: I designed a database schema that optimized for immediate convenience rather than long-term clarity, leading to tight coupling and fragile relationships that required a full rewrite.
technicalFailures.why: I prioritized speed of implementation over modeling the domain properly. Assumptions were embedded too early, and the structure could not adapt as the system evolved.
technicalFailures.lesson: Schema design is not scaffolding — it is foundation. Model the domain with patience, or pay for it in full later.
